title: Too Big to Fire? Jensen Huang Is Back at Nvidia; Questions Loom Over AI Boom & U.S.-China Relations
content:
Nvidia stock prices surged over 30% on Monday as the chip maker reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. Huang had stepped down earlier in November amid reports he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with a woman accused of spying for China. Huang and Nvidia have been central to the AI boom, and the leadership turmoil had erased trillions in value from the U.S. stock market. President Donald Trump acknowledged he had encouraged the company’s board to bring Huang back.

“The fact that our markets are so over-indexed on the AI trade, that something like three-fourths of gains in the S&P 500 this past year have been AI-related, is unsustainable,” says Aya Ibrahim, senior fellow for economic and national security at the AI Now Institute.

“The relationship is beside the point. The issue here is we have one man, one firm that many people, including those in our government, now believe are indispensable both to our economic growth and stability and to national security.”

title: Gig Work Is Invading Nursing Homes. The Risks Can Be Deadly
content:
Katie Wells, a researcher who tracks gig nursing, said a combination of factors made platforms like ShiftKey an attractive option for nursing homes. Health care facilities were struggling financially, and many of them had been taken over by private equity, which Wells said “contributed to lean staffing models that make facilities more likely to want to just plug the hole rather than invest in a larger staff.”

title: Conclusion
content: AI companies take different corporate forms and evolve over time. This report assessed whether function follows form, in the sense of whether certain business structures lend themselves to carrying out publicly minded missions more so than others. The case studies testing how various corporate vehicles walk the talk on their public missions suggest that corporate form has some bearing on how companies approach regulation, but little impact on safety and military policy. When competitive pressures and lucrative contracts are in play, financial interests prevail irrespective of the legal vehicle under which a company operates. In the competitive market that is AI, corporate structure alone cannot align companies with their mission. In fact, those very structures buckle under investor pressures, as is the case with OpenAI gradually abandoning its non-profit ethos to raise more capital.

title: AI Regulation
content: This section assesses the regulatory policy of AI companies as an indicator of their willingness to promote their public interest mission over their private interest. At the outset, it is important to acknowledge that a pro-regulatory stance is far from a perfect proxy for promoting public interest. First, not all regulation is made equal. Companies may choose to support light-touch regulation to deflect calls for stronger laws. Poorly designed regulation can also be counter-productive, actually securing the discretion and upper hand of companies under a veneer of public legitimacy.120Maroussia Lévesque, (<)em(>)Smoke and Mirrors? AI Regulation and Corporate Power(<)/em(>), 2025 U. Ill. J. Law, Tech. & Pol. 33 (2025). With these caveats in mind, regulatory policy remains a good indicator of how companies align mission and action. It conveys the extent to which they are willing to carry out their mission by complying with guardrails that purport to safeguard human well-being against AI’s downsides—even if these guardrails are imperfect. In theory, companies purporting to benefit humanity should embrace regulation. But their responses in practice say otherwise. They have been mixed at best, implying that other considerations take precedence. For example, the race among a handful of frontier labs suggests that safety takes a backseat to rapid deployment and large-scale adoption. Changing political tides in the second Trump administration and in the EU have led many companies to shed nominal calls for regulation, suggesting that these positions were more tactical than genuine.121AI Now Institute, (<)em(>)Recasting Regulation as a Barrier to Innovation(<)/em(>), in Artificial Power: 2025 Landscape Report 32 (2025), https://ainowinstitute.org/publications/1-4-recasting-regulation-as-a-barrier-to-innovation; Amnesty EU, (<)em(>)EU: AI Omnibus Deal Lawmakers Should Reject a Rollback of AI Safeguards(<)/em(>), June 11, 2026, (<)a href='https://www.amnesty.eu/news/eu-ai-omnibus-deal-lawmakers-should-reject-a-rollback-of-ai-safeguards/'(>)https://www.amnesty.eu/news/eu-ai-omnibus-deal-lawmakers-should-reject-a-rollback-of-ai-safeguards/(<)/a(>). To provide concrete examples of how companies engage with lawmakers, this section outlines their respective position on regulation based on a sample of publicly available statements. Though initiatives to regulate AI abound, the EU AI Act, California’s AI Safety regulation and the U.S. federal ban on state regulation stand out as important lenses to assess how each company under review reacts to regulatory proposals.122Artificial Intelligence Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council, 2024 O.J. (L 1689); Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act, SB-1047 (<)a href='https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB1047'(>)https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB1047(<)/a(>) (Cal. 2024) [hereinafter SB-1047]; H.R. Con. Res. 14, 119th Cong. § 43201(c) (2025), (<)a href='https://d1dth6e84htgma.cloudfront.net/Subtitle_C_Communications_4e3fbcc3bc.pdf'(>)https://d1dth6e84htgma.cloudfront.net/Subtitle_C_Communications_4e3fbcc3bc.pdf(<)/a(>) [(<)a href='https://perma.cc/8QQW-G86Y'(>)https://perma.cc/8QQW-G86Y(<)/a(>)].

title: Voluntary Scaling Policies
content: Absent AI-specific binding laws, companies devise internal policies to prevent, mitigate and redress harms associated with their advanced models. From sharing proprietary information about model weights with national safety institutes to fine-tuning for safety alignment, all companies under review apply voluntary guardrails around their products, and share information through the Frontier Model Forum. As with regulatory policy, self-imposed constraints are not a perfect proxy for companies’ willingness to uphold their stated mission to benefit humanity. These constraints can be based on a utilitarian calculus, for example avoiding regulation by showing that self-governance is sufficient. Nonetheless, what companies do of their own accord is informative as to how they implement their stated mission to benefit humanity. This section focuses on scaling policies, a subset of self-governance practices exemplifying what constraints companies are willing to impose on their own activities.

title: Revoking Corporate Charters
content: Long dormant, the state’s ability to revoke a corporation’s ability to operate has recently resurfaced as an option to rein in AI companies. Historically, corporations relied on direct state approval to exist. Governments individually approved the founding documents of corporations, known as charters, allowing them to operate for specific public purposes. In the U.S., corporations enjoyed limited liability in order to undertake major public projects such as the construction of railroads.335For a fuller history of corporations, see Tyler Halloran, (<)em(>)A Brief History of the Corporate Form and Why It Matters(<)/em(>), Fordham J. Corp. & Fin. L. Blog (Nov. 18, 2018), (<)a href='https://news.law.fordham.edu/jcfl/2018/11/18/a-brief-history-of-the-corporate-form-and-why-it-matters/'(>)https://news.law.fordham.edu/jcfl/2018/11/18/a-brief-history-of-the-corporate-form-and-why-it-matters/(<)/a(>) [(<)a href='https://web.archive.org/web/20210110171139/https://news.law.fordham.edu/jcfl/2018/11/18/a-brief-history-of-the-corporate-form-and-why-it-matters/'(>)https://web.archive.org/web/20210110171139/https://news.law.fordham.edu/jcfl/2018/11/18/a-brief-history-of-the-corporate-form-and-why-it-matters/(<)/a(>)]. Corporations carried out public service or infrastructure building with private investment, and the government maintained indirect control through the ability to revoke their charter should they digress from the public goals justifying their existence.336Daniel Hanley, (<)em(>)Pass Corporate Chartering Power to Washington(<)/em(>), Democracy J. (Sep. 8, 2021), (<)a href='https://democracyjournal.org/arguments/pass-corporate-chartering-power-to-washington/'(>)https://democracyjournal.org/arguments/pass-corporate-chartering-power-to-washington/(<)/a(>). The state’s power to revoke a corporation’s license to operate ensured public control over its activities.337Thomas Linzey, (<)em(>)Killing Goliath: Defending Our Sovereignty and Environmental Sustainability through Corporate Charter Revocation in Pennsylvania and Delaware(<)/em(>), 6 Dick. J. Env’t. L. & Pol’y 31, 36 (1997). In Delaware, where all three companies are incorporated, the Constitution still guarantees the state’s ability to revoke the charter of corporations that abuse or misuse their powers,338(<)em(>)Delaware Constitution(<)/em(>), (<)a href='https://delcode.delaware.gov/constitution/constitution-10.html'(>)https://delcode.delaware.gov/constitution/constitution-10.html(<)/a(>) (last visited Nov. 21, 2025) (“The General Assembly shall, by general law, provide for the revocation or forfeiture of the charters of all corporations for the abuse, misuse, or non-user of their corporate powers, privileges or franchises. Any proceeding for such revocation or forfeiture, shall be taken by the Attorney-General, as may be provided by law”). and the relevant statute gives courts jurisdiction to do so for “abuse, misuse or nonuse of its corporate powers, privileges or franchises.”339Del. Code Ann. tit. 8, § 284(a).

title: Military AI
content: Defense contracts are a good proxy for company self-interest. Not only are they lucrative—the Pentagon recently awarded contracts up to $200 million to each company under review—they also allow companies to stay in the good graces of regulators, presumably less inclined to impose constraints on strategic partners.223Frank Konkel, (<)em(>)Pentagon Awards Multiple Companies $200M Contracts for AI Tools(<)/em(>), Nextgov (July 14, 2025), (<)a href='https://www.nextgov.com/acquisition/2025/07/pentagon-awards-multiple-companies-200m-contracts-ai-tools/406698/'(>)https://www.nextgov.com/acquisition/2025/07/pentagon-awards-multiple-companies-200m-contracts-ai-tools/406698/(<)/a(>). However, these contracts can collide with the mission of AI companies. Debates about the potential and benefits of military AI are divisive and context-sensitive, but at minimum raise important questions about whether such applications benefit humanity in line with the stated mission of AI companies.

title: Part III. Levers to Enforce the Mission
content:
Bespoke corporate structures have not always delivered in practice when it comes to prioritizing mission over profit. However, corporate governance offers levers to hold AI companies to their word. This section explores legal tools within the corporate and securities law toolkit, listing the main recourses for each type of corporate structure under review and assessing their potential and limits
